beats.title: The Audio Loading Problem: Delays, No Caching, and a Fragile System
beats.body: GDevelop's game runtime had a persistent audio quality issue: every time a sound was played, a brand-new audio instance was created from scratch. This meant there was no reuse of already-loaded audio data, causing a noticeable delay between triggering a sound and actually hearing it. There was also no true preloading mechanism — audio files were not loaded during the game's loading screen, so the first playback always incurred a loading cost. The PR set out to fix this by caching audio instances per file, enabling reuse across plays, and adding a user-facing option to preload audio resources during the loading screen. Along the way, the contributor also converted the audio subsystem to TypeScript and reworked the internal API surface.

beats.title: Two Tensions: API Design and Breaking Changes
beats.body: The refactor surfaced two intertwined design tensions. First, the contributor initially added method chaining (fluent-style setters) to the audio sound wrapper class, mirroring the style of the underlying Howler.js library. The project owner questioned whether this was worth the cost: fluent/overloaded methods are difficult to statically type, potentially harmful to JavaScript engine optimization, and harder to reason about than explicit getter/setter pairs. Second, replacing the overloaded methods with explicit getters and setters constituted a breaking change for any game developers who had written custom JavaScript using the internal audio API. The team had to decide how much API compatibility to preserve, and whether the internal audio class should even be considered a stable public API at all.

beats.title: Position A — arthuro555
beats.body: The contributor argued in favor of initially keeping fluent method chaining for consistency with Howler.js, reasoning that users familiar with the underlying library would find the API intuitive. However, after the owner's pushback, the contributor agreed to drop the overloaded methods in favor of explicit getters and setters. The contributor also raised a concern about memory safety: if the internal sound class were treated as a public API, users could instantiate it directly in JavaScript events without the sound manager ever cleaning it up, creating potential memory leaks. The contributor felt the public API boundary should be drawn carefully to avoid exposing implementation details that could be misused. The contributor also flagged that switching from overloaded methods to getters/setters was a real breaking change for JavaScript-savvy game developers.
beats.author: arthuro555

beats.title: Position B — 4ian
beats.body: The project owner was skeptical of fluent/magic method patterns, arguing that explicit getter and setter methods are not meaningfully more verbose, are far easier to statically type (especially important given the ongoing TypeScript migration), and are friendlier to JavaScript engine optimization. On the question of whether the internal sound class should be a public API, the owner took a pragmatic stance: the team gets to decide what is and is not public, and if something is considered an implementation detail, it simply should not be exposed. If advanced users truly needed direct access to the underlying Howler object, an explicit accessor could be added later on demand rather than designing the whole API around that edge case. The owner also emphasized the value of real-world testing before merging, suggesting a beta period to catch regressions.
beats.author: 4ian

beats.question: Given the tradeoffs discussed — API ergonomics versus static typing and JIT friendliness, and the risk of breaking existing JavaScript users versus the benefit of a cleaner internal design — how would you resolve the tension between keeping compatibility with the underlying library's style and adopting explicit, type-safe patterns? And where would you draw the line between 'internal implementation detail' and 'stable public API' for a runtime used by non-expert game developers writing custom JavaScript?

beats.title: Merged: Explicit Getters/Setters Win, TypeScript Conversion Included
beats.body: The PR was merged on February 22, 2021, after roughly four months of iteration. The fluent method chaining was dropped in favor of explicit getter and setter methods, aligning with the owner's preference for static typability and clarity. The audio subsystem was fully converted to TypeScript as part of the refactor. The caching of audio instances was implemented so that the same underlying audio object is reused across multiple plays of the same file, eliminating the first-play delay. A user-facing preloading option was added to audio resources. Several rounds of bug fixes addressed issues with event listeners using incorrect scoping, zombie sound objects persisting after unloading, and undefined versus null state mismatches in sound identifiers. The internal sound class was not formally promoted to a stable public API; the team reserved the right to treat it as an implementation detail.

beats.title: Engineering Lessons
lessons: Fluent/method-chaining APIs can feel ergonomic but carry real costs in static analysis and runtime optimization; explicit getter/setter pairs are often the better tradeoff in typed, performance-sensitive codebases, even if they feel more verbose at first glance.

Deciding what counts as a 'public API' is an active architectural choice, not a passive default. Exposing internal implementation classes as public surfaces creates long-term maintenance obligations and memory-safety risks; it is better to make that boundary explicit and deliberate from the start.

Large refactors that touch runtime behavior benefit from a staged rollout with real-world testing before merging, because subtle bugs — like incorrect event listener scoping or null/undefined state mismatches — often only surface under realistic game conditions rather than in isolated unit tests.

Breaking changes to APIs used by end-users (even internal or semi-public ones) should be flagged early and explicitly, not discovered late in review; the contributor's observation that switching method styles was a breaking change for JavaScript game developers was an important signal that deserved earlier attention in the design process.
